iconic_games_note: Gillette Stadium has a genuine football (soccer) history beyond the NFL, so iconic_games is populated rather than empty. It is the home of the New England Revolution (MLS); the predecessor Foxboro Stadium hosted 1994 FIFA World Cup and 1999 Women's World Cup matches. Gillette has staged the 2003 FIFA Women's World Cup (4 matches), Copa America Centenario 2016 (3 matches), multiple CONCACAF Gold Cups, MLS Cup finals, and high-profile friendlies. Non-football note: nationally best known as an NFL stadium (six Patriots Super Bowl championship banners hang inside) but has hosted no Super Bowl. CAUTION on superlatives: the two cited attendance figures conflict in ranking — 65,612 (Inter Miami, 2024) is called the all-time record by Football Ground Guide, but the later 66,215 (France-Brazil, Mar 2026) exceeds it; neither ranking is independently confirmed and 'second-largest' was struck. Day-level dates for the 2003 WWC QF and 2016 Copa QF are approximate within the cited tournament windows.

renovations.change: Artificial FieldTurf CORE torn out and replaced with natural grass (ryegrass / Kentucky bluegrass blend) to meet FIFA's grass-surface requirement. Crews removed the turf and gravel beginning the day after the Patriots' 2025 NFL season ended, rebuilt the base with sand and porous ceramic, then laid sod (sourced from a New Jersey farm). Original early-2000s irrigation, heating and drainage systems beneath the field were found intact and reused.

city_history.significance: Foxborough, Massachusetts is a town in the Greater Boston metropolitan area, roughly 22 miles (35 km) southwest of downtown Boston and about 18 miles (29 km) northeast of Providence, Rhode Island. It was named for Charles James Fox, a British Whig MP who supported the American colonies. It is best known today as the home of Gillette Stadium, the sports and entertainment complex (with the adjacent Patriot Place) owned by the Kraft Group.
city_history.football_culture: Football culture hangs on the Greater Boston metro rather than the small town of Foxborough. Boston is a deep American sports market; the New England Patriots (NFL) and New England Revolution (MLS) both play at Gillette Stadium, and the Revolution were one of MLS's ten charter clubs, founded by Robert Kraft in 1996 and named for the region's role in the American Revolution. The region also carries deep soccer roots: Boston's Oneida Football Club (1862) is cited as the first organized football/soccer club in the United States. The predecessor, Foxboro Stadium, hosted matches at the 1994 FIFA World Cup and the 1999 Women's World Cup; Gillette has since staged the 2003 Women's World Cup, Copa America Centenario 2016, and multiple Gold Cups.

stadium_history_facts: Broke ground 24 March 2000; opened 11 May 2002. Privately financed by Robert Kraft at a cost of $325 million.
Opened as CMGI Field (11 May - 4 August 2002) before being renamed Gillette Stadium under a naming-rights deal; the FIFA neutral name for 2026 is 'Boston Stadium'.
Designed by HOK Sport (now Populous). Owned and operated by the Kraft Group.
Replaced the adjacent Foxboro Stadium (1971-2002), which hosted 1994 FIFA World Cup and 1999 FIFA Women's World Cup matches.
Home of the New England Patriots (NFL) and the New England Revolution (MLS) since 2002.

Playing surface was natural grass 2002-2006, then FieldTurf CORE artificial turf from 2006; converted back to natural grass for the 2026 World Cup (per Boston.com; the pinned Wikipedia oldid still lists FieldTurf CORE 2006-present).
Regular American-football capacity has changed over time: 68,756 (2002-2014), 65,878 (2015-2023), 64,628 (2023-present).
A separate $250 million renovation completed in fall 2023 added the 22-story Gillette Stadium Lighthouse tower with a 360-degree observation deck and a large curved outdoor video board.
Will host seven 2026 World Cup matches: five group-stage, one Round of 32, and one quarter-final (the first quarter-final, 9 July 2026).
